question: Using the customary setting of the mathematics used for quantum mechanics, is it possible to prove the existence of Gödelßs god-like entities?

5.text:
In the language in which one writes down the ordinary Hilbert-space
formalism one writes down ZF[C] plus analysis. The whole of ordinary
first order modal logic is definable in that meta-theory. In that sense
Gödel's axioms

* $P(x)\rightarrow \Box P(x)$,
* $P(x)\rightarrow P(\Box x)$,
* $E(x)$ positive,
* $\Box \exists y\,P(y)$ positive etc.,

can be written as ordinary first-order sentences in the set theoretic
language in which a separable complex Hilbert space $H$, its lattice
$\mathcal P(H)$ of closed subspaces and its self-adjoint operators are
defined, and the usual S5 proof of

$\Box\exists G\,\forall P\,[P(G)\leftrightarrow P\,{\rm positive}]$

goes through in the meta-theory. That is just the observation that
functional analysis is done in classical mathematics.

It is not a proof internal to the physics of quantum mechanics. The
physically operational logic of quantum mechanics is the orthomodular
lattice $\mathcal P(H)$ of projection operators. The propositions of the
theory are the atoms of that lattice and the lattice is not Boolean,
and in particular it is not distributive. Gödel's ontological argument
is a classical propositional/modal argument in S5. The notion of a
"positive property" used in the argument is closed under classical
implication and under the Boolean operations $\land ,\lor ,\neg$ and
under the S5 modal operators $\Box ,\Diamond$. Those closure conditions
have no model in the orthomodular propositional calculus of QM and the
modal operators $\Box ,\Diamond$ have no operational interpretation
inside the Hilbert space calculus that is used to compute probabilities,
spectra etc. Hence the ontological axioms cannot be interpreted as
physical statements about a quantum system, and the classical modal proof
does not survive passage to the quantum logical language in which
physical predictions are actually made. In the operational sense the
argument is therefore not available within the customary quantum
mechanical formalism. The formal embeddability in ZFC is vacuous.

3.text:
Customary quantum mathematics is classical mathematics. A physical
system is a separable complex Hilbert space ${\cal H}$, self-adjoint
operators on ${\cal H}$ for observables, projection lattice
${\cal P}({\cal H})$ for closed subspaces, *etc.*. All of that is
founded in ZFC set theory with the usual first order logic. In that
metatheory a formal system can be encoded and a derivation of the
form

${\rm Pos}(P)\to \Diamond {\rm Ess} P$,
${\rm Pos}(P)$,
$\square$${\rm Pos}(P)\to {\rm Pos}(P)$

*etc.*, can be carried out syntactically. In that purely syntactic
sense Gödel’s ontological argument is a theorem of S5 + the Gödel
axioms once those axioms are written as first order sentences in ZFC.
It is therefore a theorem of the set theory which underlies the
analysis used in quantum mechanics.

It is not a theorem about Hilbert space objects. The axioms

* $P1$: $P$ is positive $\to \Box P$ is positive,
* $P2$: $P$ is positive $\to P$ is necessarily positive,
* $P3$: $\Phi$ is positive $\to \exists x\, \Phi(x)$ is positive,
* $D$: $\Box \Box P\to \Box P$,

and the definition ${\rm Godlike}(x)\equiv \forall P\,[Pos(P)\to P(x)]$
are not mathematical properties of vectors, operators or projections.
They are metaphysical-modal principles about ‘positive properties’ and
□-necessity. No self-adjoint operator, no projection lattice and no
C$^{*}$-algebra encodes the predicate $Pos$ or the S5 necessity
operator in the usual quantum mechanical formalism. 

In the genuinely quantum propositional calculus the lattice of
propositions is the orthomodular lattice ${\cal P}({\cal H})$. It is
non-Boolean, indeed non-distributive for non-commuting projections.
The classical modal steps on which Gödel’s derivation rests – in
particular the unrestricted use of classical implication, distributivity
and the Boolean behaviour of $\Box$ – are not available in the
quantum logic that is the customary logical rendering of the
Hilbert-space formalism. Hence the derivation has no content as a
statement about physical observables.

In this sense there is no existence theorem for a Gödelian god-like
being inside the mathematics actually used to do quantum mechanics.
The formal derivation is only a consistency statement for a modal
theory whose primitive notions have no counterpart in ${\cal H}$,
self-adjoint operators or the ordinary analysis of physics. That is
the usual empty-formalism objection to the ontological proof. ∎

1.text:
The Hilbert space formalism of ordinary quantum mechanics is just ordinary
mathematics.  Complex vector spaces, bounded self-adjoint operators,
spectral measures etc. are all definable in ZFC + analysis. In that
language Gödel's S5 formalisation can be written down verbatim, so in the
purely syntactic sense the derivation

S5 + Positivity  ⊢  □∃x Gx

can be carried out in the same metalanguage that is used for
Hilbert-space quantum mechanics.  What the Hilbert-space mathematics does
not give you is the positivity material.

The modal theorem is conditional.  Write $P$ for a property and $Pos(P)$
for “$P$ is positive”.  Gödel needs e.g.

* $Pos(P)\rightarrow\neg Pos(\neg P)$,
* $Pos(P)\wedge Pos(Q)\rightarrow Pos(P\wedge Q)$,
* $Pos(P)\rightarrow Pos(\Diamond\exists xP(x))$,
* $Pos(NecEx)$,

and the definition $Gx\equiv\forall P\,[Pos(P)\rightarrow Px]$,
where $NecEx$ is the property of being necessarily existent.  From
S5 those axioms give

$Pos(NecEx)$, $NecEx$ positive $\rightarrow$ $\Diamond\exists x Gx$ is
positive, $\Diamond\exists x Gx$ positive $\rightarrow$ $\exists x Gx$ is
positive,
and with S5 $\Diamond\exists x Gx\rightarrow\Box\exists x Gx$, i.e. a
necessarily existent God-like being.

All of these are stipulations about an evaluative notion of positivity.
They are not statements about spectra, transition amplitudes or
projection lattices.  They are independent of ZF C, of functional analysis
and of the physical interpretation of the formalism.  Hence in the
customary QM mathematics you get at most the conditional consistency
statement

S5 + {Positivity axioms} ⊢ □∃xGx ,

not an unconditional theorem of the physics.  The existence claim is
therefore not a theorem of the Hilbert-space mathematics of quantum
mechanics; it is a conditional modal-metaphysical consequence of extra-
mathematical axioms about value.

If the mathematics of quantum mechanics is read in the von Neumann–
Birkhoff sense, i.e. in terms of the orthomodular lattice $\mathcal L(H)$
of closed subspaces and the associated quantum logic, the classical
distributive propositional inferences on which the S5 derivation rests
already fail.  In that strictly quantum-logical reading the Gödel
derivation does not even lift to the logic of the physical propositions.
That is the usual way of saying that there is no proof of a god-like
entity inside the physical mathematics itself; there is only a formal
conditional consistency result whose ontological import is extra-
mathematical.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The customary mathematics of non-relativistic quantum mechanics is the functional analysis of separable complex Hilbert spaces and the orthomodular lattice of projection operators that represent yes–no propositions about a system. That lattice is non-distributive and the propositional structure is many-valued in the sense of quantum logic, not the Boolean algebra of classical first-order predicate logic on which Gödel’s ontological argument is formulated.

Gödel’s argument requires a classical modal logic with the S5 axioms for metaphysical necessity, unrestricted comprehension of the set of positive properties, and the classical law of excluded middle for those properties. In the Hilbert-space formalism properties are represented by self-adjoint operators and propositions by projections, and the notion of a “positive property” does not have a Boolean extension that is closed under the Gödelian constructions P → □P, etc. In particular the axiom that essence is necessary, and the Converse Barcan formula used in the usual formalisation, have no natural rendering as operator identities or state-preserving maps in a C*-algebraic framework, and the orthomodular logic that governs the algebra of observables invalidates the distributive inferences Gödel uses to derive the existence axiom Gx from the definition of positive properties.

Hence there is no faithful embedding of Gödel’s full modal ontological system into the standard Hilbert-space/operator-algebra setting of quantum mechanics, and the existence of the Gödelian god-like entity cannot be derived within that customary mathematical framework.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. In the customary textbook formulation of quantum mechanics the mathematics is the standard Hilbert-space formalism over ℂ together with the usual ZFC set-theoretic background, functional analysis and measure theory. That setup is a first-order, essentially classical, mathematical universe with no built-in modal apparatus.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a theorem of modal logic S5 with a specific set of axioms about the predicate “is positive”, “is God-like”, etc. Making sense of the necessity operator □ and of the possible-worlds quantification that Kripke semantics requires demands an external modal structure, i.e. a class of accessible worlds and an interpretation of □ as truth in all accessible worlds. That modal structure is not part of the customary mathematical setting for quantum mechanics, which contains no semantics for metaphysical modality and no privileged interpretation of □ as physical necessity.

One can of course formalize the axioms of the ontological proof in the background set theory used for QM, but the proof is not a theorem of the Hilbert-space formalism or of ordinary quantum mechanical mathematics itself. It remains an external metatheoretical statement about an added modal logic, and so it cannot be established as an internal consequence of the customary mathematics used for quantum mechanics without importing an essentially non-quantum, non-standard modal apparatus.

2.text:
The formal apparatus that is normally used for quantum mechanics is ordinary
classical mathematics. A separable complex Hilbert space, its self-adjoint
operators, spectral measures, etc., are all defined in ZFC, in fact in
Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the usual first order logic and the
classical quantifiers. It is in that same set theoretic background that
first order and higher order modal logic is usually formalised.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a theorem of modal logic S5 from a
small set of metaphysical premisses about the notion of a positive
property.  In the usual formulation one postulates

* P is positive iff ...,
* necessarily,  P is positive -> not-P is not positive,
* necessarily, if P is positive then necessarily P is positive,
* necessarily, if P is positive then P is possibly exemplified,
* and the usual modal axioms for S5.

From those premisses one obtains  $\Diamond \exists x Gx \rightarrow \Box 
\exists x Gx$ and with the further axiom $\Diamond \exists x Gx$ the
conclusion $\Box \exists x Gx$, a being possessing all and only the
positive properties. That is a purely syntactic derivation. It can be
carried out in any system that contains the modal and second order
logic needed to talk about properties. ZFC, and hence the functional
analysis that underlies Hilbert space theory, is more than enough to
express and formalise the derivation.

What the formalisation does not do is give you a physical or
metaphysical proof of existence. The derivation is conditional on the
positivity axioms and on the modal conception of necessity that is built
into S5. The mathematics of quantum mechanics supplies a language for
operators and states, it does not supply, and cannot supply, a
justification for the axioms

$ P $ positive $\rightarrow \Box P $ positive,
$\Box\, \forall P\, [\,P $ positive $\rightarrow \Diamond \exists x\, Px\,]$

and the choice of which properties count as positive. In particular
Hilbert space theory is classical. It does not force you into quantum
logic, and it does not add any new non-classical ontological principle
that would make the premisses of Gödel’s argument true in the physical
world.

So in the purely formal sense the Gödel derivation can be written down
inside the same set-theoretic foundations that are used to define a
Hilbert space. In any substantive sense – a proof of the actual
existence of a maximally great or God-like entity from the physics of
quantum mechanics – there is nothing more to be gained from the Hilbert
space formalism than there is from ordinary mathematics. The argument
remains a conditional consistency result from unproved metaphysical
axioms, and the physics of quantum mechanics licenses none of those
axioms. That is the usual way of saying the proof does not prove
existence.
